q: You are taking over a 22 m motor yacht whose flybridge compass sits 1.2 m to starboard of the centreline. What must be true for it to read her heading?
a: Its lubber line is parallel to the fore-and-aft line
o: Its lubber line points straight at the stem head
It is moved onto the centreline before you sail
A small offset is added to every heading read
why: A compass reads the heading anywhere aboard if its lubber line is parallel to the keel; aiming it at the bow from off-centre builds in an error.

fig.title: Flybridge steering compass
lines: Compass 1.2 m to starboard of the centreline
Lubber line: to be checked before sailing

q: You find this in the steering compass at 0300, 60 M from land. What do you do?
a: Cross-check it with another compass; refill it ashore
o: Top up the bowl at sea with the fresh water aboard
Carry on — a bubble does not affect the card
Steer by the GNSS COG alone until you reach port
why: A big bubble makes the card stick and jump; refill with the maker's fluid ashore, and check headings against another compass meanwhile.

fig.title: Steering compass, 0300
lines: Bubble about 2 cm across under the glass
Card sticks, then jumps, in a turn

q: On a two-day beat you check the steering compass against the satellite compass, upright in harbour and now heeled at sea. What do you do for the rest of the beat?
a: Use the deviation found heeled on this tack
o: Use the upright card — heel does not change deviation
Apply the 090°C error to every heading you steer
Steer by the hand-bearing compass from the cockpit
why: Heeling error comes from iron below the compass tilting with the boat: it is largest on N and S headings, so check the deviation heeled.

q: You are fitting these at the new helm console, with the steering compass in the middle. Which must go furthest from the compass?
a: The VHF loudspeaker
o: The radar display
The plotter display
The autopilot control head
why: Each maker states a compass safe distance; the loudspeaker's magnet needs the most, 1.4 m here.

q: You make this alteration at night and read the steering compass for the log. When do you write down the new heading?
a: Once the card has settled on the new course
o: At once, while the card is still turning
After taking 20° off for the overshoot
Never — log the plotter's COG instead
why: After a fast turn the damping liquid keeps swirling and drags the card; wait until it settles on the new course.

q: Your Biscay crossing runs between these two compass roses on the passage chart. Which variation do you use halfway across?
why: Update each rose: 12 years × 10'E = 2° less west, so 2°20'W and 0°20'W; halfway, 1°20'W.
ref: Compass — variation and its annual change

q: You are halfway across on this small-scale passage chart. Where do you take the variation from?
a: The isogonic line at your position, updated
o: The rose on the departure harbour's chart
Nowhere — it is only shown near the coast
The plotter's value for the departure port
why: Small-scale charts give variation as isogonic lines with a year and an annual change; read the one at your position and update it.

fig.title: Passage chart 1:1 000 000
lines: No compass rose on this sheet
Your position: midway, 70 M from land

q: You use this rose on an old Channel chart in 2026. Which variation do you apply?
why: 15 years × 8'E = 2°00' less west: 1°45'W − 2°00' = 0°15'E — the variation has passed through zero.
ref: Compass — variation and its annual change

q: Forty miles offshore you check the steering compass with the sun's bearing over its shadow pin. What is its deviation on this heading?
why: Sun 227°T + 3°W = 230°M; the compass reads 228°, 2° low, so deviation is 2°E (C + dev = M).
ref: Compass — deviation by the sun's azimuth

q: The compass swing before a 400 M passage gives this card. What do you do?
a: Have a compass adjuster correct it with magnets
o: Sail on the card — 7° is fine if you apply it
Correct it yourself with the magnets at sea
Steer by the GNSS COG and ignore the compass
why: Deviation this large comes from the boat's own magnetism; an adjuster reduces it with corrector magnets, then swings again for a new card.

fig.title: Swing results, steering compass
lines: Passage next week, much of it at night

q: These changes were made since last season's compass swing. Which one means the deviation card can no longer be trusted?
a: C — the new wiring and instruments at the helm
o: A — the new anchor chain in the forepeak
B — the new antifouling on the hull
D — the new set of sails
why: Deviation comes from iron and current near the compass; new wiring and instruments beside it change it, so swing again.

fig.title: Since the last swing
lines: A: new anchor chain, forepeak, 14 m away
C: helm rewired, new instruments by it

q: You take the sun's bearing over the steering compass between two tabled times. What deviation do you write down for this heading?
why: At 1022 the azimuth is 140° + 12/20 × 5° = 143°T, 145°M; the compass reads 148°, 3° high: deviation 3°W.
ref: Compass — deviation by the sun's azimuth

q: On this passage the steering compass disagrees with the card after the alteration. What is the likely cause?
a: Retained magnetism from long on one heading
o: Variation changing along the passage
Heeling error on the new heading
A fault in the satellite compass
why: Steel held long on one heading picks up magnetism that lingers for hours after a turn; recheck the deviation until it settles.

fig.title: 24 m steel motor yacht
lines: Compass 3° off the card for some hours
Calm, no heel; checked by sat compass
Variation from the chart for here

q: You swing the compass in a slow circle off the coast, sighting this distant peak on each heading. What deviation do you find on 090°C?
why: Deviation averages out round the circle: the mean of the eight bearings, 104°, is the magnetic bearing; 101° on 090°C reads 3° low — 3°E.
ref: Compass — swinging on a distant mark

fig.title: Swing on a distant peak
lines: Magnetic bearing of the peak unknown

q: You are fitting the autopilot's fluxgate sensor on a 22 m sailing yacht. Where do you put it?
a: Low, near the middle, away from iron and cables
o: At the masthead, far from all the iron below
In the engine room, where it is out of the way
On the stern arch, beside the radar scanner
why: A fluxgate is magnetic and feels motion: mount it low near the centre of pitch and roll, clear of iron, motors and cables.

q: You set up the radar overlay and MARPA like this, and the targets plot in the wrong places. What do you fix?
a: Fit a heading sensor — COG is not the heading
o: Turn up the radar gain until they settle
Set the plotter display to north-up
Slow down so that the COG steadies
why: Overlay and MARPA need the boat's heading; COG is her track over the ground, here 25° off the bow in the cross-tide.

q: The owner of this yacht wants one heading source for the autopilot, radar and AIS. Which do you fit?
a: A satellite compass on the radar arch
o: A fluxgate sensor inside the wheelhouse
The plotter's GNSS COG output
A second magnetic compass on the mast
why: A satellite compass takes true heading from two GNSS antennas: no deviation from the steel, and it works when stopped.

fig.title: 24 m steel motor yacht
lines: Often at slow speed or stopped

q: You are about to enter the area in this warning. Which heading can you still trust inside it?
a: The magnetic steering compass
o: The satellite compass
The plotter's COG readout
The autopilot's GNSS heading
why: Jamming knocks out every GNSS-based heading; the magnetic compass needs no signal and no power.

fig.title: NAVAREA warning
lines: Radius 120 M round the position given

q: You check the steering compass against the satellite compass on a steady heading. What is its deviation on this heading?
why: Satellite compass 210°T + 4°W = 214°M; the steering compass reads 217°, 3° high, so deviation is 3°W.

q: Making a night landfall, this bearing of the light ahead is your only position line. What does it give you?
a: Whether you are on track, not how far to go
o: How far to go, not whether you are on track
A fix, once you add the log reading to it
Nothing until a second light comes up
why: A bearing along your track checks the cross-track error only; distance to go needs a line that cuts across it.

q: Northbound across the Bay, the sounder first finds the bottom at 190 m at 0420. Which part of your DR does this check?
a: The distance run — the edge lies across the track
o: The cross-track error — the edge runs along it
Both — a single sounding is a full fix
Neither — depths this great are not charted
why: A contour is a position line; this one cuts your track at right angles, so it checks the distance run (log and along-track stream).

q: Seventy miles off, over charted depths of 4,200 m, the sounder shows this at night. What is it?
a: A deep scattering layer, not the seabed
o: An uncharted bank — alter course at once
A double echo of the real seabed
The bottom — the chart is in fathoms
why: At night plankton and fish form a layer a few hundred metres down that gives a soft, moving echo; it is not the bottom.

fig.title: Sounder, 0130
lines: A soft, fuzzy trace at 380 m
It rises and falls slowly over the hour

q: The racon on the offshore light float shows like this on your radar. Which range do you plot?
a: 16.0 M — the inner end of the flash
o: 16.8 M — the middle of the flash
17.5 M — the outer end of the flash
14.5 M — the inner end less its length
why: A racon replies as soon as it is triggered: its code starts just beyond the float, so take the range to the inner end of the flash.

fig.title: Racon on the radar
lines: Inner end of the flash: 16.0 M

q: These two lighthouses come in transit at dawn. How good is the transit as a position line?
a: Weak — they barely open as you move off it
o: Exact — a transit has no error at any range
Useless — a transit needs daymarks, not lights
Better than near in — the further, the finer
why: A transit is sensitive only while you are within about three times the distance between the marks; here you are fifteen times it.

fig.title: Transit at dawn
lines: In line when 15 M off the front one

q: Your radar is head-up and you read the lightvessel's bearing from it. Which true bearing do you plot?
why: True heading 212° + 2°E − 3°W = 211°T; add the relative bearing 047°: 258°T.

q: You take a radar bearing of this headland's edge for a fix. How do you correct it?
a: Move it 1° towards the land
o: Move it 1° towards the sea
Move it 2° towards the land
Leave it — EBL bearings are exact
why: The beam paints an echo half a beamwidth wider each side, so a land edge shows 1° too far out to sea; correct towards the land.

fig.title: Radar bearing of a headland
lines: EBL set on the echo's eastern edge
Land lies to the west of the edge

q: At 20 kn at night you want a three-light fix with the hand-bearing compass. In which order do you take the bearings?
a: A, C, then B
o: B, A, then C
A, B, then C
C, B, then A
why: Take the lights ahead and astern first — their bearings change slowly — and B, nearest the beam, last; then note the time and log.

q: You take a hand bearing of this light in these conditions. How do you get a bearing you can use?
a: Take several readings and use their mean
o: Take the first reading when the card stops
Take the largest reading of the swing
Add 8° to the reading for the swing
why: In a seaway the card swings about the true bearing; several readings, averaged, give the best value.

fig.title: Hand bearing at night
lines: Light 12 M off, flashing every 5 s

q: You can take only two of these bearings before the haze closes in. Which pair gives the best fix?
a: B and C
o: A and D
A and C
C and D
why: B and C cut at 81°, nearest 90°; A and D are 178° apart — almost the same line, the worst cut of all.

q: In this sea your hand-bearing compass can be 3° out. How far can the position line from this light be off?
why: 1 in 60: 3° at 20 M is 20 × 3 ÷ 60 = 1.0 M either side of the line.

fig.title: Bearing of a distant light
lines: Light 20 M off by the DR

q: Your fixes keep coming out like this. What is the likely cause?
a: The same error in every bearing, such as deviation
o: One of the three lights wrongly identified
Random errors — take the centre each time
The stream setting you between bearings
why: A cocked hat that keeps its size and side although the marks are right points to a constant error; one correction to all three closes it.

fig.title: Three fixes, 2100–2140
lines: Each cocked hat 0.4 M, same size and side
Taken within a minute each time

q: You work a running fix on one light from 2200 to 0100 in this stream. How do you transfer the 2200 position line?
a: 26.2 M along 252°T
o: 27.0 M along 250°T
27.8 M along 248°T
25.4 M along 257°T
why: Water track 27.0 M on 250°T plus three hours of stream (010° 1.2, 030° 0.8, 200° 0.6) gives the ground run: 26.2 M on 252°T.

fig.title: Running fix, 2200 to 0100
lines: Water track 250°T at 9.0 kn, no leeway

q: You doubled the angle on the bow of this light from 22½° to 45°. How far off will you pass it abeam?
why: Doubling the angle: the distance off at 45° equals the run, 6.0 M; abeam it is the run × sin 45° = 4.2 M.
ref: Position fixing — doubling the angle on the bow

fig.title: Doubling the angle
lines: No stream, no leeway, course steady

q: You took this four-point bearing with the stream dead astern. How far off the light are you now it is abeam?
why: The distance abeam equals the run over the ground: log 3.8 M + 1.5 kn × 24 min (0.4 h) = 4.4 M.

fig.title: Four-point bearing
lines: 0212 light 45° on the port bow, log 31.4

q: You take a four-point bearing of this light with the stream across your track. How far off are you when it is abeam?
a: Plot it — the rule fails in a cross-set
o: 5.0 M — the log run, as the rule says
4.0 M — the run less the 1.0 M set
6.0 M — the run plus the 1.0 M set
why: The four-point rule needs the stream along the track; a cross-set skews the triangle, so plot both bearings and the ground track.

fig.title: Four-point bearing, 0300–0330
lines: Light 45° on the bow, then abeam
Stream 2 kn, setting you towards the light

q: After this strike you need a fix at dawn. Which method does not rely on either compass?
a: Horizontal sextant angles between the three
o: Three bearings with the hand-bearing compass
A radar range and EBL bearing of one light
A running fix on the nearest lighthouse
why: Two horizontal sextant angles between three charted marks fix you with no compass at all; every bearing needs a compass you trust.

fig.title: After a lightning strike, 0200
lines: Steering and hand compass differ by 20°
Three charted lighthouses in sight at dawn

q: You want a radar fix off this oilfield. Which echo do you use?
a: X — a fixed platform at its charted position
o: Y — the nearer echo gives a better range
Both, then average the two positions
Y — it is named in the NAVAREA warning
why: A production platform is fixed and charted; a drilling rig moves between sites, so its position is only as good as the latest warning.

fig.title: Radar, 0350
lines: Echo X, 11 M: charted production platform
Echo Y, 9 M: nothing charted there
NAVAREA: a drilling rig working in the area

q: As these two lights come in transit you want a second position line. Which do you take?
a: The radar range of A
o: The hand bearing of C
A sounding with the echo sounder
None — the transit alone is a fix
why: A's range cuts the transit at 90° and radar ranges are accurate; C's bearing cuts it at only 25°, and the depth tells nothing here.
ref: Position fixing — transit and a second line

fig.title: 0420: lights A and B in transit
lines: C: a hand bearing would cut it at 25°
A's radar range would cut it at 90°
Depths all round: a flat 70–75 m

q: You are on this bearing of the light; the sounder reads below its transducer. Where on the line are you?
a: B — at the 43 m sounding
o: A — at the 42 m sounding
C — at the 46 m sounding
D — at the 49 m sounding
why: Charted depth = sounding 45.0 + transducer 1.0 − tide 3.0 = 43.0 m, so you are at B.
ref: Position fixing — depth and a bearing

q: You want an independent fix as you pass this wind farm. What do you use?
a: Radar ranges of two charted corner turbines
o: The AIS turbine symbols round you on the plotter
The centre of the farm's block of radar echoes
A hand bearing of the nearest unlit turbine
why: AIS targets are drawn relative to your own GNSS position, so they cannot check it; ranges of charted, lit corner turbines can.

fig.title: Offshore wind farm
lines: Corner turbines lit and marked singly
AIS shows each turbine as a virtual aid
Radar: a dense block of echoes

q: At night, 20–25 M off, you can see these lights. Which do you take bearings of?
a: A and D — the two lighthouses
o: B and D — the brightest pair
A and C — they cut nearest 90°
B and C — the nearest to the track
why: Use lights charted and kept for mariners; an aero light is not maintained for you, and a flare stack is not charted at all.

fig.title: Lights in sight, 0130
lines: B: Aero Al Fl WG, 12 M inland
C: glow of a flare stack, uncharted

q: You have these four positions for 0300, a few cables apart. Which do you trust most?
a: B — ranges of steep cliffs, cutting well
o: A — three lines beat any two
C — one light, so no misidentification
D — its HDOP is excellent
why: Ranges of steep cliffs are accurate and cut at 80°; bearings at 20 M err 0.3 M a degree, a 3 h run piles up errors, and the depth rules out D.
ref: Position fixing — which fix to trust

fig.title: Four fixes, 0300
lines: B: radar ranges of 2 cliffs, 8 M, cut 80°
C: running fix on one light, 3 h run

q: You are watching for this light from the cockpit of a 22 m sailing yacht. At what distance do you expect it to rise?
why: 2.08 × (√64 + √3.0) = 2.08 × (8 + 1.73) = 20.2 M, inside the 24 M nominal range, so it rises there.

q: Closing this light, the flybridge watch saw it rise at 2310. When will it rise for the helmsman at the lower helm?

fig.title: Landfall light, 2310
lines: Light height 49 m; nominal range 25 M
Eye: flybridge 7 m, lower helm 3 m
Heading straight for it at 15 kn

q: On this night the light rises much further off than the formula says. What do you make of the rising distance?
a: Abnormal refraction — do not use it as a range
o: The radar range must be 6 M out
The charted height of the light is wrong
Use the formula's 20 M; it overrides radar
why: Warm air over a cold sea bends light down and lets it be seen far beyond the computed range; rising ranges hold only in normal conditions.

fig.title: Landfall, 0140
lines: Warm air over a cold sea, flat calm
Formula gives 20 M for your eye

q: At 0240 these all agree on your position, but the depth does not. Why is their agreement no cross-check?
a: They all take their position from one GNSS receiver
o: AIS and DSC are less accurate than the plotter
The sounder cannot be trusted at these depths
The chart was surveyed by GNSS, so it must agree
why: Plotter, AIS and DSC are fed by the same receiver: if it is wrong they are all wrong together. Check with depth, DR, radar or lights.

fig.title: 0240, 90 M offshore
lines: Plotter, AIS and DSC radio: same lat/long
Sounder 112 m; charted depth there 160 m
DR from 2200 puts you 6 M south

q: Your GNSS behaves like this at 0315. What do you do?
a: Go back to DR from the last good fix
o: Restart the receiver and use what it gives
Trust the plotter — it shows many satellites
Steer for the new position to check it
why: Jumps, a frozen speed and a wrong date point to spoofing; plot from the last good fix and fix by depth, radar and lights.

fig.title: GNSS, 0315
lines: SOG reads 0.0 kn; the date shows 2019

q: You fix your position by three lights at 0300 on an offshore passage. What do you enter in the log?
a: Time, position, how it was fixed and the log
o: Time and lat/long — the plotter keeps the rest
Position and course — the time is on the plot
The position and the watch leader's name
why: The log must let anyone rebuild the plot: the time, the position, how it was fixed and the log reading.

q: This warning comes in at 0230. Which entry in your log do you restart the plot from?
a: 0130 — the last fix before the spoofing
o: 0200 — the latest GNSS fix in the log
0000 — only a visual fix can be trusted
Now — the plotter's position at 0230
why: GNSS fixes after 0145 are worthless; because the log records how each fix was made, you can see 0130 was the last good one.

q: You plot your 0400 position from the 0300 fix, the log and the compass, allowing for the stream and leeway. How do you mark it and log it?
a: A triangle, logged as an EP
o: A circle with a dot, logged as a fix
A short cross line, logged as a DR
A square, logged as a waypoint
why: A position from log, compass, stream and leeway is an estimated position: a triangle on the chart, 'EP' in the log.

q: Before an Atlantic passage you swing the compass of your 24 m motor yacht against her satellite compass. Which deviation do you apply on the night course?
why: M = T + 2°W: 138°M on 135°C is 3°E, 177°M on 180°C is 3°W; a third of the way, 150°C: 3°E − 2° = 1°E.
ref: Compass — deviation card from a swing

q: Your helmsman has steered 210°C since 0200 by the card from last month's swing. Which true heading do you use for the 0300 EP?
why: Two-thirds of the way from 180°C to 225°C: 1°E − 4° = 3°W, so 207°M; + 2°E variation = 209°T.

q: At midnight you take the helm on the flybridge after a day at the lower helm. Which deviation card do you use now?
a: The flybridge compass's own card
o: The lower helm's card — it is the master
The mean of the two cards
None — the flybridge compass needs none
why: Each compass sits in its own spot among the iron and wiring, so each has its own deviation and its own card.

fig.title: Two steering compasses
lines: Lower helm: card from the swing in May
Flybridge: its own card, same swing

q: Before a night passage the crew stow the tender as shown. What do you do before relying on the flybridge compass?
a: Check its deviation again on the night course
o: Nothing — the card covers any stowage
Add the card's largest error to every course
Apply the lower helm's card to it instead
why: A steel hull and an engine 2 m from the compass change its deviation; the card was made without them there, so check it again.

fig.title: Tender stowage tonight
lines: Steel-hulled tender with a 60 hp outboard
Card swung with the tender on the foredeck

q: You are taking two yachts out after the winter. Which compass must be swung again before the first offshore passage?
a: B — her hull's magnetism has changed
o: A — a GRP hull loses its card in winter
Both — every card expires in a year
Neither — nothing near either compass moved
why: A steel hull long on one heading, and hammered or welded, takes on new permanent magnetism, so her deviation changes; GRP has none.

fig.title: After the winter
lines: A: GRP sloop, ashore, nothing changed aboard
B: steel motor yacht, 5 months in a shed
B: bow north all winter, hull welded

q: The compass adjuster fits these to the binnacle of your steel motor yacht. What are they for?
a: To cancel the deviation from the steel hull
o: To correct the heeling error alone
To steady the card in a seaway
To shield it from the radar's signal
why: The spheres and the Flinders bar offset the magnetism induced in the hull's soft iron; the magnets offset its permanent part.

fig.title: Fitted to the binnacle
lines: A soft-iron Flinders bar in front

q: You need bearings of three lights for a fix from your steel motor yacht. What do you take them with?
a: The steering compass, with its azimuth ring
o: The hand compass at the bow, clear of the bridge
The hand compass, adding 10° for the steel
The plotter, as bearings to the light symbols
why: On steel the hand compass is deflected everywhere; the adjusted steering compass, with its card, gives bearings you can trust.
ref: Compass — bearings on a steel yacht

fig.title: Steel motor yacht, 0130
lines: Hand-bearing compass: 6–15° out about the decks
Azimuth ring aboard for the steering compass

q: You have run the new fluxgate compass's calibration circles, then check it on a transit. What do you do?
a: Set a 4° heading alignment offset
o: Run the calibration circles again
Move the sensor further from the steel
Use it as it is — fluxgates need no card
why: The same error on every heading is the sensor's alignment, not magnetism; calibration cannot see it, so set the offset.

fig.title: Fluxgate check on a charted transit
lines: Steering compass agrees with the transit

q: At 25 kn the autopilot's fluxgate heading does this in every fast turn. What is happening?
a: The turn swings its sensor off the level
o: Its deviation card is out of date
The variation changes as she turns
The engines' current deflects it at speed
why: In a fast turn the sensor's gimbal swings off level and picks up the field's vertical part; trust the heading once she is steady.
ref: Electronic compass — heading error at speed

fig.title: Fluxgate heading, fast turns
lines: Swings 15° past the new course in the turn
Settles about 10 s after she steadies
Steady course: agrees with the steering compass

q: The new satellite compass is wired to the autopilot. Which compass still needs a deviation card?
a: The magnetic steering compass
o: The satellite compass
Both of the compasses
Neither — the plotter corrects both
why: A satellite compass measures true heading from GNSS signals and has no deviation; the magnetic compass still has its own.

q: You take a range and an EBL bearing of the same headland for a fix. How far off could each position line be?
a: Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±0.3 M
o: Arc ±0.3 M; EBL line ±0.05 M
Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±0.4 M
Arc ±0.05 M; EBL line ±1.5 M
why: Across the EBL line: 12 M × 1.5° ÷ 60 = 0.3 M, six times the range arc's 0.05 M — trust the range more.

q: The radar ranges of the two islands cross at X and Y. Which is your position?
a: X — the rough bearing of A fits only X
o: Y — ranges beat a rough bearing
Either — two ranges always fix you
Midway between the two crossings
why: From X, island A bears about 333°T; from Y it would bear 290°T. Even a rough EBL tells the two crossings apart.

q: Between bearings of the same light at 2200 and 0000 you alter course at 2300. By what do you move the first position line?
a: 11.9 M along 086°T
o: 12.1 M along 070°T
13.2 M along 056°T
12.0 M along 052°T
why: Add both water legs and both hours of stream: 7.0 M 040° + 7.0 M 100° + 1.4 M 160° + 2.0 M 180° = 11.9 M on 086°T.

q: You work this running fix on a single light. How far could the transferred line be out from the stream alone?
why: An error of 0.4 kn for 2.5 h moves the transferred line up to 1.0 M either way, and the fix with it.

fig.title: Running fix, 2130 to 0000
lines: Bearings of one light, 2.5 h apart
Atlas rate here good to ±0.4 kn

q: Closing the coast in the morning, you measure the vertical sextant angle of this lighthouse. How far off is it?

fig.title: Vertical sextant angle, 0710
lines: MHWS 4.6 m; height of tide now 1.6 m

q: You check the sextant's index error, then take a vertical sextant angle of this light. How far off are you?
why: IE on the arc is subtracted: 39.0'. Height now 88 + 3.6 = 91.6 m; 1.854 × 91.6 ÷ 39.0 = 4.4 M.

fig.title: Vertical sextant angle, 0640
lines: MHWS 4.4 m; height of tide 0.8 m
Sextant reads 0°42.0'; IE 3.0' on the arc

q: You want a distance off this lighthouse by vertical sextant angle. Which angle do you measure?
a: From the light down to the shoreline below it
o: From the light down to your sea horizon
From the tower's foot up to its top
From the cliff top down to the shoreline
why: The charted elevation runs from MHWS to the light, so measure from the light to the waterline at its foot, inside your horizon.

fig.title: Lighthouse on a cliff top
lines: Cliff foot 3 M off, well inside your horizon

q: You are closing the Brittany coast at low water springs, watching for this light from the flybridge. At what distance do you expect it to rise?
why: At low water the light stands 38 + (12.2 − 2.2) = 48 m up: 2.08 × (√48 + √4) = 18.6 M, inside its 23 M range.

fig.title: Light list and almanac
lines: Light 38 m above MHWS, nominal 23 M
MHWS 12.2 m; height of tide now 2.2 m

q: Your EP puts this light 31.0 M dead ahead at 0200. When do you tell the flybridge lookout to expect it?

fig.title: Landfall light, 0200
lines: Light 52 m above MHWS, nominal 24 M
MHWS 4.8 m; height of tide 1.6 m
Flybridge eye 5.0 m; 11 kn straight at it

q: Northbound in fog over the shelf, you log these soundings every 2 M. Which track have you been on?
a: Track B
o: Track A
Track C
None of them
why: Only on B does the canyon fall on the third sounding: 142, 148, then 405 m, then back to 155 and 160 m.

fig.note: Soundings every 2 M, from the south

q: Out of sight of land, you have a line of soundings taken at equal distances along a steady course. How do you get a position from them?
a: Draw them to scale on tracing paper, slide to fit
o: Average them and find that depth on the chart
Take the deepest one as a fix
Plot each on the DR and take the mean
why: Mark the soundings along a course line on tracing paper at the chart's scale, then slide it over the chart, course kept, until they match.

fig.title: Line of soundings
lines: Passage chart of the shelf, tracing paper

q: You have this single bearing of the light and a good sounding. How much does the sounding add?
a: Little — the depth hardly changes along the line
o: A fix — where the line meets the 84 m sounding
A check of your distance off the light
A second line cutting the bearing at 90°
why: The contours run along this bearing, so the depth is about 84 m all along it; a sounding helps only where contours cross the line.

q: 60 M offshore at 0200 the GNSS status page shows this. How do you treat the position?
a: As unchecked — cross-check it by other means
o: As good — an HDOP of 1.6 is excellent
As lost — switch the receiver off
As wrong — go back to DR at once
why: With RAIM unavailable the receiver cannot flag a faulty satellite; a good HDOP proves nothing, so check by radar, depth and DR.

q: On your steel motor yacht these two fixes disagree by 0.8 M. Which do you work from?
a: GNSS and radar — the hand bearings were deflected
o: The visual fix — its cocked hat is small
The mean of the two fixes
Neither — wait for daylight to fix
why: Hand bearings by a steel wheelhouse share one deflection: a neat cocked hat in the wrong place. Two independent sources agree.

fig.title: Fixes at 0300
lines: GNSS: agrees with radar ranges of two cliffs
Visual: hand bearings of three lights
Small cocked hat, 0.8 M from the others

q: Your three-light fix lies 0.5 M from the GNSS position. What do you conclude?
a: They agree — within the visual fix's own error
o: The GNSS is 0.5 M out — plot the visual fix
One of the lights must be misidentified
Average them: the truth lies midway
why: At 22 M, ±2° is ±0.7 M across each line, so a visual fix there is only good to about that; 0.5 M is no disagreement.

fig.title: Fix check, 0230
lines: Lights 18–22 M off, cut 60° and more
Visual fix 0.5 M from the GNSS

q: Making a night landfall with these lights ahead, you close all of them at the same rate. Which do you expect to see first?
a: Light C
o: Light A
Light B
Light D
why: Each shows at the lesser of its nominal and geographic range: A 14, B 14.0, C 19.0, D 10 M. C needs 11 M more; the rest 13–14 M.

fig.title: Lights ahead · your eye 3 m
lines: A: 85 m, nominal 14 M · 28 M off
B: 25 m, nominal 25 M · 27 M off
C: 55 m, nominal 20 M · 30 M off
D: 12 m, nominal 10 M · 24 M off

q: Closing the coast at night, you see this light change from white to red at 0215. What does it give you?
a: A position line on the sector's charted edge
o: A fix — the change marks a single point
Nothing — sector colours give no position
Your distance off the light
why: Where the colour changes you are on the sector edge, a line from the light on a charted bearing; good to a degree or so, not a fix.

fig.title: Sectored light, 0215
lines: Seen white, then red, as you head SE

q: Watching for the landfall light from the cockpit, you see this. What does it tell you?
a: You are at about its rising range
o: The light is weak — report it
Haze is thickening between you
You are inside its obscured sector
why: A light that shows only from the wave crests is on your horizon: you are at its rising distance for your height of eye.

fig.title: Landfall, 0410
lines: Light seen only on the top of each swell
Characteristic matches the light you expect

q: Before a night landfall after 140 M, you write up a card for each light you expect. What goes on it?
a: Its characteristic, rising range and expected bearing
o: Its name, its colour and the chart number
Its height, its tower and its fog signal
Its range and the date of its last check
why: The watch must know what to look for, when it should rise and where: the characteristic, the rising range and the bearing.

q: 90 M offshore in open water, your mate wants to fix every 10 minutes all night. What do you tell him?
a: Hourly is enough here; keep the lookout
o: Every 10 minutes, as near hazards
Once a watch, since GNSS is on
Only when the GNSS alarm sounds
why: With no hazard for 40 M an hourly fix and EP keep you safe; save frequent fixes for the coast, and the crew for the lookout.

fig.title: Night watch, 0100
lines: 90 M from land, nearest hazard 40 M off

q: Your EP can be out by 10% of the distance run since the last fix. How often must you fix to keep to your rule past this bank?
a: Every 1 h 30 min
o: Every 3 h 00 min
Every 9 min
Every 1 h 50 min
why: Half the gap is 1.8 M; at 10% that takes 18 M of running, which at 12 kn is 1.5 h — 1 h 30 min.

fig.title: Passing a bank at night
lines: Rule: fix before the error reaches half the gap

q: Reading the night's log to restart the plot, which entry falls short of a proper fix record?
a: C — no method and no log reading
o: A — a fix by lights is logged as an EP
B — GNSS fixes are not logged
D — radar fixes go on the chart only
why: A fix record needs the time, position, how it was fixed and the log; C gives no method to judge it and no log to run on from.

q: At 0315 you get only one bearing of a light before it is lost in rain. How do you record it?
a: Plot the line with its time; log the bearing and log
o: Log it as a fix where it cuts the DR track
Leave it out — one line is no position
Log it as an EP with the light's name
why: A single position line is worth keeping: draw it with the time, and log the bearing and the log reading so it can be run on later.
ref: Recording fixes — a single position line

q: Your only position line is this bearing of the light, and your EP lies off it. Where on the line do you put yourself?
a: At the point on it nearest the EP
o: Where your course line crosses it
Where it reaches the light's range
Nowhere — stay on the EP till a fix
why: With one line and an EP, take the point on the line nearest the EP: the smallest shift that fits both.

q: You note the log as this light comes 26½° and then 45° on the bow. How far off will you pass it abeam?
why: For 26½° then 45° the distance abeam equals the run between them: 46.1 − 40.3 = 5.8 M.

fig.title: Light on the bow, steady course

q: Your three-light fix at 0200 gives this cocked hat. What do you make of its size?
a: About what the bearing errors give at this range
o: Too big — one light must be wrong
Too big — the compass must be swung
Small enough to treat as a point
why: ±2° at 20–24 M is ±0.7–0.8 M across each line, so a 1.2 M hat is normal; treat it as an area, clear of danger here.

q: To save time, the crew offers to swing the compass against the plotter's COG on passage. Will that give a good card here?
a: No — the current can put COG 10° off the heading
o: Yes — round a full circle the current cancels
Yes — at 6 kn a 1 kn current hardly shows
No — COG is true and the card is magnetic
why: A 1 kn current at 6 kn turns the track up to 10° (sin⁻¹ 1/6) off the heading; a card needs heading — a transit, the sun, a sat compass.

fig.title: Swing by GNSS COG?
lines: Plan: slow circle, compass vs COG

q: You hold 245°T for 150 M across these isogonic lines, deviation nil on this heading. Which compass course do you give the helm?
a: 250°C at the start, 247°C at the end
o: 240°C at the start, 243°C at the end
250°C for the whole crossing
247°C at the start, 250°C at the end
why: 245°T + 5°W = 250°C at the start; + 2°W = 247°C at the end — ease the course a degree as each isogonic line is crossed.

q: After 140 M on EP you sight a light ahead with the right characteristic, but off its expected bearing. Is it your light?
a: Likely — a 7 M error can swing it up to 20°
o: No — 17° off puts you 17 M from the EP
No — a 7 M error moves it 7° at most
No — the bearing should agree within 3°
why: From 20 M off, a 7 M error in the EP can shift the light's bearing by up to sin⁻¹(7/20) ≈ 20°; 17° fits, so confirm it by timing it.

fig.title: Landfall, 0350
lines: EP could be 7 M out after 140 M

q: 100 M offshore, beyond soundings and out of sight of lights, how do you check each hourly GNSS fix?
a: Against the EP worked from the last fix
o: Against the AIS position of a passing ship
There is no check — accept the GNSS
Against a second reading of the same receiver
why: Offshore the cross-check is the EP from the last fix by log, compass and stream; a gap that grows means find out why.

fig.title: Mid-Biscay, 0200
lines: Depth 4,500 m; no lights in sight
Log, compass and the stream known

q: On a clear night you check the steering compass on the Pole Star. What is the deviation on this heading?
why: Polaris 359°T + 3°W = 002°M; the compass reads 004°, 2° high, so the deviation is 2°W.
ref: Compass — deviation by the Pole Star

q: Three lights are in sight for a hand-bearing fix as you run at 18 kn. Which do you take first, second and last?
a: B, C, then A
o: A, B, then C
C, A, then B
A, C, then B
why: B is nearly ahead and C on the quarter: their bearings change slowly. A is nearly abeam and changes fastest, so take it last.

q: You can take radar ranges of any two of these. Which pair gives the best fix?
a: A and C
o: A and D
A and B
B and D
why: Range arcs cut at the same angle as the targets' bearings differ: A and C are 90° apart; A–D and B–D are near-reciprocal, A–B 15°.

q: At 0100 you had only a radar range of an island; at 0230 you take a bearing of a light. How do you run the 0100 range on?
a: Move the island by the run; redraw the arc
o: Move the arc's nearest point along the track
Add the run to the 8.0 M range
You cannot — wait for two lines at once
why: A transferred circle keeps its radius: move its centre by the ground run since 0100 and draw the 8.0 M arc again from there.

fig.title: Running fix with a range
lines: Ground track and run for 1.5 h known

q: Closing the coast on this bearing of the light, you see nothing well after its rising time. Why?
a: You are inside its obscured sector
o: Its rising range is less than you worked out
The light is out — report it and carry on
Haze has cut its luminous range
why: Light-list bearings are from seaward: on 238°T you are in the 210°–255° arc where the land hides it.

q: Your noon sun check finds 4°W on 200°C, where the card says 1°W. What do you do with it?
a: Log it and use 4°W on this heading for now
o: Ignore it — an adjuster made the card
Average the two and use 2½°W
Apply 3°W extra on every heading
why: A fresh check beats an old card on that heading: log it, use it and check again; a gap that stays means a new swing.

q: Your helmsman wants to apply the deviation card to the COG on the plotter. What do you tell him?
a: The card is for the magnetic compass only
o: Apply it, then add the variation
Apply it twice for the plotter's error
Apply it only when the GNSS is weak
why: COG comes from GNSS and has no deviation; the card corrects only the magnetic compass it was made for.

q: The headland's echo lies between the 4 M and 6 M rings. How do you get its range for the fix?
a: Put the VRM on the echo and read it off
o: Estimate it by eye between the rings
Take the nearer ring, 4 M, to be safe
Take it as 5 M, midway between
why: Fixed rings give only a rough guide; the VRM set on the echo measures the range to the radar's full accuracy.

fig.title: Radar, 6 M scale
lines: Headland echo between the 4 and 6 M rings

q: You take radar ranges of two charted rocks. The arcs cross twice; which crossing is your position?
a: 6.0 M from A on 143°T
o: 6.0 M from A on 037°T
8.0 M from A on 127°T
6.0 M from A on 323°T
why: A 6-8-10 triangle: the crossings lie 3.6 M east of A and 4.8 M either side of AB. The 85 m sounding picks the south one: 143°T from A.

fig.title: Radar ranges, 0420
lines: Rock B lies 10.0 M due east of rock A
Range of A 6.0 M · range of B 8.0 M
Sounder 85 m: south of AB 80–90 m

q: At 0100 you crossed the 200 m shelf edge; at 0300 a light bears 040°T. How do you run the 200 m line on for the fix?
a: 16.0 M along 184°T
o: 16.0 M along 180°T
16.0 M along 176°T
16.0 M along 182°T
why: A contour runs on like any position line: 16.0 M on 180° by log plus 1.0 M on 270° of stream = 16.0 M along 184°T.

fig.title: Contour and bearing, 0100–0300
lines: Water track 180°T at 8.0 kn, no leeway
